newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-SPANISH CHARGE AHEAD FROM THE BASELINE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SPANISH CHARGE AHEAD FROM THE BASELINE.

text.p: Spaniards Carlos Moya and Felix Mantilla led a charge by clay-court specialists into the last eight at the Australian Open on Sunday as the baseline brigade intensified their challenge.
Their fourth-round victories in searing heat guaranteed that Spain will achieve its best ever Grand Slam performance away from the slow red clay courts of Europe.
The Spanish charge on the Rebound Ace hardcourt prompted American second seed Michael Chang, another fourth-round winner on Sunday, to declare: "The Spanish are coming".

Chang, a former French Open champion and another counter-puncher from the back of the court, dropped his first set of the tournament before overpowering unseeded Ukrainian Andrei Medvedev 4-6 6-2 6-2 6-1 on Centre Court.
Unseeded Moya, who upset defending champion Boris Becker in the first round, added Swede Jonas Bjorkman to his list of victims, winning a marathon five-setter 6-3 1-6 3-6 6-2 6-4.
His victory, which will propel the flamboyant 20-year-old into the world's top 20 for the first time, set up a clash with Mantilla, guaranteeing Spain at least one semifinalist.
Mantilla, who attributed the improvement to a collective decision to practise more on hardcourts in recent months, proved too strong for unseeded American MaliVai Washington, winning 7-5 6-2 6-1.
Tenth seed Albert Costa, Spain's number one, could add to his country's success story when he plays eighth seed Wayne Ferreira of South Africa in a fourth-round encounter on Monday.
In the last men's match on Sunday, Chilean ninth seed Marcelo Rios took his furthest step in a Grand Slam by beating seventh seeded Swede Thomas Enqvist 4-6 6-4 7-6 6-7 6-3.
Rios improved on his fourth round at last year's French Open when he prevailed in three hours and 15 minutes.
But it was the Spaniards who caused the biggest stir, reversing the trend of recent history with their performance in the year's first grand slam.
No Spaniard has reached the quarter-finals in Melbourne since the tournament switched from grass to the slower Rebound Ace hardcourt surface in 1988.
"I think that the press of all the world don't think the Spanish can play on this surface but we now have two players in the quarter-finals," Mantilla said.
"We've been clay court players but I think we are showing that we can play on all kinds of surfaces," Moya said in his post-match news conference.
After his shock exit Becker, the sixth seed and a renowned serve-and-volley exponent, said the courts and balls were slower in Melbourne this year and would help clay court exponents.
But Chang, the world number two behind top seed and fellow American Pete Sampras, disagreed. He said the conditions were unchanged from previous years.
Chang outlined his own theory to explain the sudden improvement by Spanish players.
"I think the Spaniards were pretty content to just stay on clay but they realise that now, in order to make an impact on tour, they have to expand on to other surfaces as well," he said.
